Paragraph:
Translation: Our strength is immeasurable, and we are perfectly protected by Grandfather Bhisma, whereas the strength of the Pandavas, carefully protected by Bhima, is limited.

Purport (Excerpt): Herein an estimation of comparative strength is made by Duryodhana. He thinks that the strength of his armed forces is immeasurable, being specifically protected by the most experienced general, Grandfather Bhisma. On the other hand, the forces of the Pandavas are limited, being protected by a less experienced general, Bhima... Duryodhana was always envious of Bhima because he knew perfectly well that if he should die at all, he would only be killed by Bhima. But at the same time, he was confident of his victory on account of the presence of Bhisma...
Situation/Problem_Faced: Duryodhana makes a direct, biased comparison between the two armies. He concludes his forces are 'immeasurable' under Bhisma's command, while dismissing the Pandavas' strength as 'limited' under Bhima's command, despite his deep-seated, subconscious fear of Bhima.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: He utilizes confirmation bias to reassure himself. He highlights his greatest asset (Bhisma) while minimizing his greatest fear (Bhima), thereby artificially inflating his own confidence and suppressing his anxiety.
Outcome/Resolution: Duryodhana solidifies a false sense of security, convincing himself that victory is assured based on this skewed comparative analysis.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Ahamkara (The ego desperately constructing a narrative of superiority to protect itself)
Matsarya (Envy; specifically, Duryodhana's lifelong toxic envy of Bhima's strength)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The verse exposes the blindness caused by envy and ego. Duryodhana's material calculations are fundamentally flawed because they are rooted in his personal hatred and fear. He trusts in the protection of a mortal general (Bhisma) while ignoring the divine protection of the Pandavas, demonstrating a complete lack of spiritual vision.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Duryodhana is exhibiting intense psychological compartmentalization and projection. He actively suppresses his subconscious terror of Bhima (his known harbinger of death) by overvaluing Bhisma's protection. This rationalization allows him to transform his deep-seated anxiety and envy into a fragile, arrogant confidence.
